page: Vultr voc-s-2c-16gb-320s-amd is an x86_64 architecture server within the Optimized Cloud Compute family. It features 2 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 1 physical AMD EPYC core with 2 threads. The system is equipped with 16.0 GB of system memory, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per core. Local storage consists of a 320 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance includes 1 complimentary public IPv4 address.

Benchmark data shows strong single-core performance, with stress-ng single-core CPU performance ranking in the top 10% and Geekbench single-core scores in the top 25%. Single-threaded gzip compression and bzip3 decompression also register in the top 25%. However, multi-core and multi-threaded capabilities are limited by the dual-vCPU configuration, resulting in weak multi-core Geekbench and Passmark CPU scores. Memory bandwidth is average for large blocks but weak for small cached blocks.

The server exhibits poor performance in high-throughput scenarios, such as static web serving and large-model LLM inference. Database operations, including Redis SET and Passmark database benchmarks, also fall into the bottom 25%. Consequently, this configuration is best suited for memory-intensive but compute-light workloads, single-threaded processing tasks, or lightweight background workers rather than high-concurrency web serving or database hosting.
description: Vultr voc-s-2c-16gb-320s-amd is an x86_64 server in the Optimized Cloud Compute family, featuring 2 dedicated vCPUs from a single physical AMD EPYC core, 16.0 GB of RAM, and a 320 GB NVMe SSD. It delivers strong single-core performance, with stress-ng single-core results in the top 10% and strong single-threaded compression and decompression benchmarks. However, the dual-vCPU constraint limits multi-core efficiency, leading to lower scores in multi-threaded Geekbench, Passmark, and database operations. Static web serving throughput and LLM inference for larger models are also weak. This resource profile offers a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core, making it qualitatively cost-efficient for memory-bound, single-threaded workloads, lightweight background tasks, and development environments that require dedicated CPU allocation but do not demand high multi-threaded concurrency.
